passage:
Wasim had a fresh joke every morning, and the joke was always Manjula's blushing or Jahnavi's thick glasses. On Tuesday he pretended to fan his red face in front of the whole row, and Manjula's ears burned. After that she stopped raising her hand, ate lunch in a corner of the library and told her mother she had a stomach ache.

Jahnavi felt something hotter. All through maths she pictured tipping his bag into the drain and watching him cry. The picture scared her a little, so at break she took her notebook to the teacher and read out what she had imagined. The teacher thanked her for saying it, said the anger made sense but the drain did not, and walked her to the staffroom to talk about it.

That evening Manjula, waiting on her building's stairwell, heard Wasim's father shouting on the floor below and then Wasim going very quiet. Something about his jokes made sense to her, though it did not make them fair. Next morning, when he started again, she said, "Stop, that is not funny," in a flat voice, picked up her books and went to sit near the teacher's table.

qa.q: Where did Manjula eat her lunch after the teasing began?
qa.a: She ate her lunch in a corner of the library.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi's way of handling her anger differ from Manjula's way of handling her hurt, and what did Manjula's stairwell moment add?
qa.a: Jahnavi's anger became a picture of the drain, but she told the teacher instead of acting on it. Manjula first withdrew, then said stop and went to sit near the teacher. Hearing Wasim's father shout explained his jokes to Manjula, but it did not make them fair.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she read her imagined drain scene out to the teacher?
qa.a: She was angry, and also frightened by how strong the picture was, which is why she wanted an adult to hear it.

qa.q: What could Manjula do next if Wasim keeps teasing her even after she says stop?
qa.a: She could keep walking away and tell the teacher or her mother each time, since understanding why he behaves this way does not mean she has to put up with it.

grounding: The same teasing by one classmate is shown through a target who withdraws then answers calmly, one who imagines revenge but tells an adult, and one who sees the hurt behind the bully.

passage:
On Friday evening the lamp was lit in the corner of the flat, and Parul, not yet two, was carried in by her father. The bell rang, and she stopped mid-squirm. Her eyes went to the little flame, which shook whenever someone breathed near it, and her mouth fell open.

Nani was already sitting on the mat. She patted her knees and Parul climbed up, warm and heavy, leaning her head on Nani's chest while the chanting began. Nani's voice hummed right through her back. When the others folded their hands, Parul copied them, wobbling, palms slapping together instead of joining. Her brother Zubin rang the bell and she clapped at the sound and laughed. Nobody hushed her.

Midway she got restless and slid down to poke at a marigold. Her mother simply moved the plate a little way off and let her be. A few minutes later Parul crawled back into Nani's lap, tugged at her bangle and stayed there till the last verse, thumb in mouth, while incense curled up toward the ceiling.

qa.q: What did Parul do when the bell rang?
qa.a: She stopped squirming and looked at the little flame.

qa.q: How do the three moments in the evening, copying the folded hands, gazing at the flame and settling in Nani's lap, fit together?
qa.a: Parul copies the family's folded hands and claps at the bell, she stares at the flame and the incense, and she feels loved in Nani's lap. She joins because the family does and because she feels safe, so the prayer becomes belonging.

qa.q: What does Parul's return to Nani's lap suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt secure and loved with Nani, comfortable enough to wander off and come back.

qa.q: How could the family keep prayer time pleasant for a toddler who gets restless?
qa.a: They could let her wander, move breakable or hot things out of reach as her mother did, and welcome her back without pressure to sit still.

grounding: A toddler's imitation of family gestures, her wonder at flame and sound, and the affection of a grandmother's lap all appear in one prayer evening.

passage:
The email from HR reached Gurpreet at 4:10, and by 5:00 his desk was in a cardboard box. Six years of late launches, and the same director who thanked him at the anniversary dinner had signed the letter. He sat in the car park with his hands shaking, feeling lied to. Then he opened his laptop, and instead of the angry draft he wanted, he wrote to HR asking for the terms in writing and to his old manager asking for a reference.

Hansa, laid off in the same round, went home and said nothing. She kept leaving the house at nine in a work shirt and sitting in a cafe, sure that this said something rotten about her. On the fourth day she called her cousin and told her.

Gurpreet's parents took the news quietly at dinner, then his mother asked about the rent. He laid out his savings and his plan on paper. Darshan, his father, stayed silent, then pushed the roti toward him.

The next week, still furious about the party photos from the record quarter, Gurpreet sent HR three exact questions about notice, severance and his rights. He posted nothing online.

qa.q: How many years had Gurpreet worked at the company?
qa.a: He had worked there for six years.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet's and Hansa's first reactions to the layoff differ, and what did each eventually do?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt lied to and turned his anger into written terms, a reference and exact questions to HR. Hansa felt ashamed and hid the layoff in the cafe until she told her cousin on the fourth day. Both then took a step involving someone else.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she kept leaving the house in a work shirt?
qa.a: She was ashamed, treating the layoff as a judgement on her worth and not wanting anyone to know.

qa.q: What could Hansa do now to steady her days while she searches for work?
qa.a: She could keep the trusted person close, build a simple daily routine and treat the job search as her new work, remembering the layoff came from a company round rather than her worth.

grounding: One layoff round is shown through a colleague's betrayal and anger, another's shame and hiding, and a family's anxious reliance on the income.

passage:
Bhavna's cousin's birthday party had moved to the terrace by ten. Someone passed round a vape, and Pranav, fifteen, felt every eye on him. "Don't be boring," a boy said. Pranav grinned, said "I'm the designated snack guard," grabbed the chips and went to the far corner. Nobody pushed further.

Near the stairs, an older boy with a sports bag was handing out free vapes and pills wrapped in foil to the younger ones. "Take one, bring your friends, we can sort out selling later," he said to Bhavna. Something in her stomach turned cold; it felt like bait. She shook her head, went down the stairs, and texted her aunt to pick her up. Her aunt arrived within twenty minutes.

Kamal, Pranav's friend, had been quiet all evening. Pranav noticed Kamal's hands shaking and remembered that Kamal had been using something almost every weekend for months. He didn't lecture. He said, "I'm worried about you, and I'll come with you to talk to your sister," and Kamal, staring at the floor, said maybe.

That night, Pranav lay awake thinking he was curious about it too, but that curiosity and wanting to look cool were tangled, and he wanted to read what it really does to a growing brain first.

qa.q: What did Pranav say to get out of the pressure at the party?
qa.a: He said he was the designated snack guard and took the chips to the far corner.

qa.q: How is the older boy's offer to Bhavna different from the pressure Pranav felt from the boy who called him boring?
qa.a: The boy calling Pranav boring wanted him to join in, while the older boy offered free items as a hook to bring Bhavna and her friends into selling. Pranav could joke his way out, whereas Bhavna needed to leave and tell an adult.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he lay awake that night?
qa.a: He felt curious but unsure, aware that some of his interest came from wanting to look cool, so he wanted facts before deciding.

qa.q: What could Pranav do next for Kamal if Kamal keeps using and gets worse?
qa.a: He could keep showing care without lecturing, encourage Kamal to accept help, and tell a trusted adult if Kamal's safety is at risk.

grounding: One party is used to show a friend-group offer, an older peer's hook, personal curiosity and a friend's protective concern about the same subject.

passage:
The call came while Urmila was making tea. "Ma'am, this is your bank, and your account is frozen unless you confirm the code in ten minutes." The caller even knew her name. Her chest tightened, but something felt wrong; she hung up, dialled the number printed on her card and was told the bank had made no such call.

Joseph was not so lucky. Three weeks before, he had paid a "registration fee" for a job offer and lost most of his internship savings. He told nobody because he could already hear the jokes. It was Urmila who found him at the canteen with his phone face down and asked, "You look awful. What happened?" Joseph talked, and within an hour they were at the cyber cell counter with screenshots.

On the way, Joseph was seething. "I'm going to message this guy from another number and trap him myself," he said. Urmila shook her head. "Give the police what you have. Chasing him alone could cost you more."

That evening Yusuf sent the group a link. "Guaranteed profit, doubles in a week, my uncle's friend made a lot." Urmila did not forward it. She wrote back, "Where did you get this? Show me who runs it," and added a heart so he would know she still liked him.

qa.q: What did Urmila do after the caller said her account would be frozen?
qa.a: She hung up, dialled the number printed on her card, and learned the bank had not called.

qa.q: How did Joseph's silence and Urmila's quick call lead to different outcomes?
qa.a: Urmila paused and checked through an official number, so she lost nothing. Joseph stayed silent out of fear of jokes and lost savings, until speaking up got him to the cyber cell.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he wanted to trap the scammer himself?
qa.a: He was furious and wanted revenge, though that plan could bring more loss.

qa.q: How could Urmila respond to Yusuf so that the friendship stays but the scheme does not spread?
qa.a: She can question him calmly about the source, refuse to forward it, and show him warmly that she is not judging him, which is what she did.

grounding: One friend group meets a scam through a spoofed call, a hidden loss, an angry urge to retaliate and a friend forwarding a too-good scheme.

passage:
Chinmay heard it through the bedroom wall: his parents arguing in low voices about fees and a loan. His stomach dropped, and then a guilty thought came, that his tuition was the reason. Next morning he asked his mother, "Is money really tight? Can I do something?" She told him a little and said the rest was for grown-ups to sort out. He decided to sell his old comics at school, and stopped there.

At lunch Ganga showed off her new phone and a photo from a trip to the hills. Chinmay smiled and said nothing, feeling bitter enough to notice it. Later he thought, I have my cricket team and my own room, and I am not going to borrow money just to pretend.

That night an ad flashed on his screen: "Turn ten rupees into a thousand with our betting app." His thumb hovered. Then he closed it and told his mother.

On Sunday Vinita, a relative, came for tea and mentioned with a pleasant smile that the term fees had been paid "just as we agreed". Chinmay's face went hot; he was thankful and ashamed in the same breath. He said, "Thank you, truly. I will pay it back one day," and meant it. Afterwards he asked his parents quietly whether they could gently ask Vinita to leave the fees out of tea-table talk. His father nodded slowly and said he would.

qa.q: What did Chinmay decide to sell at school?
qa.a: He decided to sell his old comics.

qa.q: How did Chinmay's reaction to the betting ad differ from his reaction to Vinita's remark about the fees?
qa.a: He closed the betting ad and told his mother, because the ad was a stranger's offer of quick money. Vinita, a relative, was helping with the fees, so Chinmay felt thankful and ashamed together and asked his parents to gently set a boundary.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when Ganga showed her new phone?
qa.a: He felt bitter, and he noticed it instead of hiding it or acting on it.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do next if he starts to feel guilty about the family's money worries again?
qa.a: He could ask his parents what is happening, offer help that fits a child's role like selling comics, and remember he is not the one who has to fix the debts.

grounding: One family's money trouble is seen through a teen's worry and guilt, an online get-rich ad, envy of a friend and a relative's help that brings both thanks and shame.
